records.sourceFile: Effects of multiple cold-water immersion during pre-season on recovery performance in under-20 male soccer players - A randomized controlled trial.pdf

paper.citation: Effects of multiple cold-water immersion during pre-season on recovery performance in under-20 male soccer players: A randomized controlled trial. Journal of Bodywork and Movement Therapies. 2024;40:563-568.
paper.abstract: A randomized controlled trial tested whether repeated cold-water immersion during a nine-day preseason period improved recovery in 23 under-20 male soccer players.
paper.tldr: Daily cold-water immersion lowered creatine kinase but did not improve jump, strength, or perceived recovery versus control.
paper.methods: Twenty-three under-20 male soccer players completed a nine-day preseason period and were randomized to 10 minutes of 10 C cold-water immersion after training or control recovery. Creatine kinase, vertical-jump performance, strength, and perceived recovery were tracked.
paper.findings: Creatine kinase was approximately 280 U/L lower with cold-water immersion, while vertical jump, strength, and perceived recovery did not differ meaningfully between groups.
paper.limitations: The sample was small, male, under-20, and observed over a short preseason period. The biomarker change did not translate into demonstrated functional or perceptual benefit.
paper.practicalImplications: Cold-water immersion may reduce a muscle-damage biomarker during dense preseason training, but practitioners should not assume it improves performance recovery or how athletes feel.
paper.athleteDev: Use selectively when short-term biomarker reduction is a priority, while preserving active recovery, sleep, nutrition, and training-design strategies that have broader developmental value.
paper.rtp: The study did not examine injured athletes or return-to-play decisions; creatine kinase alone should not be used as a clearance marker.

records.sourceFile: Wake up call for collegiate athlete sleep- narrative review and consensus recommendations from the NCAA Interassociation Task Force on Sleep and Wellness.pdf

paper.citation: Wake up call for collegiate athlete sleep: narrative review and consensus recommendations from the NCAA Interassociation Task Force on Sleep and Wellness. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2019;53(12):731-736.
paper.abstract: An NCAA interassociation task force synthesized evidence and expert consensus into recommendations for supporting sleep and wellness in collegiate athletes.
paper.tldr: Collegiate programs should monitor time demands, screen sleep at preparticipation, educate athletes and staff, and provide referral pathways.
paper.methods: A multidisciplinary task force used a narrative evidence review and consensus process to formulate collegiate-athlete sleep recommendations.
paper.findings: The group recommended annual assessment of time demands, routine sleep screening during preparticipation evaluation, sleep education, and access to qualified clinical referral when concerns are identified.
paper.limitations: This is a narrative consensus statement rather than a systematic review or intervention trial, so recommendations are not comparative-effectiveness estimates.
paper.practicalImplications: Build sleep support into program operations: identify schedule pressures, screen consistently, teach practical sleep behaviors, and define escalation routes for clinical concerns.
paper.athleteDev: Treat sleep as a trainable health and performance behavior supported by the environment, not solely as an athlete-compliance issue.
paper.rtp: Sleep screening can identify barriers that affect rehabilitation and recovery, but the statement does not provide injury-specific return-to-play thresholds.

records.sourceFile: Real world fatigue testing in professional rugby union - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Real world fatigue testing in professional rugby union: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2023;54(4):855-874.
paper.abstract: A systematic review examined fatigue-monitoring responses after professional men's rugby-union match play and meta-analyzed outcomes with sufficient comparable data.
paper.tldr: Post-match soreness rises reliably, but most other commonly used fatigue markers have uncertain or inconsistent responses.
paper.methods: Thirty-seven professional male rugby-union studies were included and 14 contributed to meta-analysis of post-match fatigue and recovery markers across the first 96 hours.
paper.findings: Muscle soreness increased during the 96 hours after match play. Pooled effects for many other subjective, neuromuscular, biochemical, and endocrine markers were non-significant or too heterogeneous for confident interpretation.
paper.limitations: Protocols, match contexts, sampling times, and outcome definitions varied substantially. Evidence was concentrated in professional male rugby union.
paper.practicalImplications: Use a small, repeatable monitoring battery and interpret athlete trends in context rather than expecting one universal fatigue test to dictate recovery decisions.
paper.athleteDev: Longitudinal individual baselines and consistent testing conditions are more useful than isolated post-match values.
paper.rtp: These post-match fatigue measures were not validated as injury rehabilitation or return-to-play criteria.

records.sourceFile: Effect of the length of the microcycle on the daily external load, fatigue, sleep quality, stress, and muscle soreness of professional soccer players - A full-season study.pdf

paper.citation: Effect of the length of the microcycle on the daily external load, fatigue, sleep quality, stress, and muscle soreness of professional soccer players: A full-season study. Sports Health. 2022;15(5):695-699.
paper.abstract: A full-season observational study evaluated how professional soccer microcycle length related to daily external training load and athlete-reported wellness.
paper.tldr: Microcycle length changed how training load was distributed, but reported fatigue, sleep, stress, and soreness were largely unchanged.
paper.methods: Professional soccer players were monitored across a competitive season, with external load and daily wellness outcomes compared across microcycles of different lengths.
paper.findings: External load distribution varied by the number of days between matches, whereas fatigue, sleep quality, stress, and muscle soreness showed little corresponding difference. Match-day loads were generally similar.
paper.limitations: The observational single-team context limits causal inference and may not transfer to other leagues, schedules, or athlete populations.
paper.practicalImplications: Adjust the placement of training load when match spacing changes, but continue monitoring individual wellness because group averages may appear stable.
paper.athleteDev: Microcycle planning should balance exposure opportunities with schedule constraints instead of assuming shorter cycles automatically worsen perceived recovery.
paper.rtp: The study informs team scheduling but does not establish rehabilitation load progressions or return-to-play criteria.

records.sourceFile: Effects of consecutive domestic and international tournaments on heart rate variability in an elite rugby sevens team.pdf

paper.citation: Effects of consecutive domestic and international tournaments on heart rate variability in an elite rugby sevens team. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2019;22(5):616-621.
paper.abstract: An elite rugby-sevens team was monitored across consecutive domestic and international tournaments to compare heart-rate variability and subjective recovery responses.
paper.tldr: Athletes felt worse after both tournaments, while the clearest heart-rate-variability decline occurred after international travel and competition.
paper.methods: Ten Olympic-level rugby-sevens players completed heart-rate-variability and self-report monitoring around domestic and international tournaments with similar match-load exposure.
paper.findings: Self-reported recovery worsened following both tournaments. Heart-rate variability declined more clearly after the international tournament despite broadly similar match load, suggesting contextual effects such as travel.
paper.limitations: The sample was only ten athletes from one elite team, and tournament context cannot be separated cleanly from travel and other environmental factors.
paper.practicalImplications: Interpret autonomic and self-report monitoring together and account for travel, time zones, and tournament logistics when planning recovery.
paper.athleteDev: Build individualized travel routines and use repeated within-athlete measures rather than population cut points.
paper.rtp: Heart-rate variability changes after competition are not an injury-clearance test and should not independently determine return to play.

records.sourceFile: A Strategy to Inform Athlete Sleep Support From Questionnaire Data and Its Application in an Elite Athlete Cohort.pdf

paper.citation: A Strategy to Inform Athlete Sleep Support From Questionnaire Data and Its Application in an Elite Athlete Cohort. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2022;17(10):1532-1536.
paper.abstract: Questionnaire responses from a large elite-athlete cohort were clustered to identify recurring sleep-problem profiles that could help target support.
paper.tldr: Combining sleep quality and behavior questionnaires produced three practical support profiles, but they are exploratory rather than diagnostic.
paper.methods: Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index and Athlete Sleep Behavior Questionnaire data from 412 elite athletes in 27 sports were analyzed with k-means clustering.
paper.findings: Three distinct profiles emerged, separating athletes with broadly favorable sleep, sleep-quality concerns, and behavior-related support needs.
paper.limitations: The analysis was cross-sectional, self-reported, and dependent on the selected clustering method. Profiles do not diagnose sleep disorders.
paper.practicalImplications: Use questionnaires to triage education and follow-up, then confirm concerns through conversation or clinical assessment when indicated.
paper.athleteDev: Profile-based support can make sleep education more relevant than delivering the same advice to every athlete.
paper.rtp: The profiles may identify recovery barriers during rehabilitation but are not return-to-play thresholds.

records.sourceFile: Professional athletes have poorer sleep quality and sleep hygiene compared with an age-matched cohort.pdf

paper.citation: Professional athletes have poorer sleep quality and sleep hygiene compared with an age-matched cohort. Clinical Journal of Sport Medicine. 2020;31(6):488-493.
paper.abstract: A cross-sectional cohort study compared sleep duration, quality, regularity, environment, and hygiene in professional athletes and age-matched non-athletes.
paper.tldr: Professional athletes reported longer sleep but poorer quality, regularity, and sleep environments, with more napping than comparators.
paper.methods: Questionnaire-based sleep characteristics were compared between 184 professional athletes and 101 age-matched clinic comparators.
paper.findings: Athletes reported longer sleep duration but more disturbance, less regular schedules, poorer sleep environments, and more napping than the comparison cohort.
paper.limitations: Cross-sectional self-report data cannot establish causation, and the clinic comparison group may not represent the general population.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not equate time in bed with good sleep. Review schedule consistency, environment, disturbances, and nap practices with athletes.
paper.athleteDev: Sleep coaching should target routines and context as well as duration.
paper.rtp: Poor sleep may complicate recovery, but this study does not provide injury-specific prognostic or clearance criteria.

records.sourceFile: Sleep quality in elite athletes - Normative values, reliability and understanding contributors to poor sleep.pdf

paper.citation: Sleep quality in elite athletes: Normative values, reliability and understanding contributors to poor sleep. Sports Medicine. 2021;52(2):417-426.
paper.abstract: A large elite-athlete study described Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index values, test-retest reliability, and questionnaire components associated with poor sleep scores.
paper.tldr: About half of elite athletes screened as poor sleepers; sleep latency and perceived quality were important contributors, and changes under three points may be noise.
paper.methods: Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index responses from 479 elite athletes were analyzed for normative patterns, contributors, and repeatability, including estimation of a minimum detectable change.
paper.findings: Fifty-two percent scored at least five on the PSQI. Sleep latency and subjective quality were prominent contributors, and the estimated minimum detectable change was three points.
paper.limitations: The PSQI is a screening questionnaire rather than a clinical diagnosis, and group normative values may obscure individual or sport-specific context.
paper.practicalImplications: Use repeated scores and component-level discussion; avoid treating small score fluctuations as meaningful change.
paper.athleteDev: Focus support on the specific behaviors or barriers driving an athlete's score instead of labeling the athlete from a total score alone.
paper.rtp: PSQI results can flag a recovery concern but should not be used as a standalone return-to-play test.

records.sourceFile: Sleep interventions in elite sport - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Sleep interventions in elite sport: A systematic review. South African Journal of Sports Medicine. 2025;37(1).
paper.abstract: A systematic review synthesized intervention studies intended to improve sleep outcomes in elite athletes.
paper.tldr: Sleep education most consistently increased sleep quantity; other interventions showed promise but the evidence was heterogeneous.
paper.methods: Thirty-two elite-sport intervention studies covering education, light exposure, supplements, cold exposure, mindfulness, and related approaches were reviewed.
paper.findings: Sleep-education interventions most consistently improved sleep quantity. Positive findings were also reported for several other approaches, but effects varied across methods and outcomes.
paper.limitations: Study designs, sports, interventions, and sleep measures were heterogeneous, with many small samples and limited replication.
paper.practicalImplications: Start with individualized sleep education and environmental or scheduling changes; treat specialized interventions as context-dependent trials that require monitoring.
paper.athleteDev: Use behaviorally specific, athlete-centered sleep plans and evaluate whether the chosen intervention changes the intended outcome.
paper.rtp: Sleep interventions may support rehabilitation recovery, but no universal intervention or sleep threshold was validated for return to play.

records.sourceFile: The effect of alcohol on subsequent sleep in healthy adults - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: The effect of alcohol on subsequent sleep in healthy adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Sleep Medicine Reviews. 2025;80:102030.
paper.abstract: A systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated how alcohol consumed before sleep affects objective and subjective sleep outcomes in healthy adults.
paper.tldr: Alcohol disrupted REM sleep even at low doses; higher doses shortened sleep latency, but many other outcomes remained uncertain.
paper.methods: Twenty-seven controlled studies of alcohol exposure and subsequent sleep in healthy adults were synthesized, with meta-analysis where outcomes were comparable.
paper.findings: Rapid-eye-movement sleep was disrupted even at doses approximating two standard drinks. Higher doses shortened sleep latency, while evidence for several other sleep outcomes was inconsistent or uncertain.
paper.limitations: Participants were healthy adults rather than athlete-specific cohorts, and alcohol dose, timing, and sleep measurement varied between studies.
paper.practicalImplications: A faster onset of sleep after alcohol should not be interpreted as better recovery; discuss the likely REM-sleep cost even at relatively low intake.
paper.athleteDev: Include alcohol timing and dose in recovery education, especially around travel, evening competition, and dense training periods.
paper.rtp: The evidence concerns sleep physiology, not injury clearance; alcohol use may be a modifiable recovery factor during rehabilitation.

records.sourceFile: Antioxidants for preventing and reducing muscle soreness after exercise- a Cochrane systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Antioxidants for preventing and reducing muscle soreness after exercise: a Cochrane systematic review. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018;54(2):74-78.
paper.abstract: A Cochrane systematic review evaluated antioxidant supplementation for preventing or reducing delayed-onset muscle soreness after exercise.
paper.tldr: Antioxidants produced, at most, a very small soreness reduction below the review's threshold for practical importance.
paper.methods: Fifty studies involving 1,089 participants compared antioxidant supplements with placebo or control for post-exercise muscle soreness and adverse effects.
paper.findings: Pooled reductions in soreness were smaller than the prespecified minimal important difference. Forty-seven studies were judged at high risk of bias, and adverse-event reporting was sparse.
paper.limitations: Most trials had high risk of bias, interventions and exercise models varied, and the evidence base provided limited safety information.
paper.practicalImplications: Routine antioxidant supplementation should not be expected to create a meaningful reduction in post-exercise soreness.
paper.athleteDev: Prioritize training progression, sleep, and adequate nutrition over supplements with trivial average benefit and uncertain long-term adaptation effects.
paper.rtp: The review did not evaluate injury healing or return-to-play outcomes; soreness reduction is not evidence of tissue readiness.

records.sourceFile: Compression Garments and Recovery from Exercise- A Meta-Analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Compression Garments and Recovery from Exercise: A Meta-Analysis. Sports Medicine. 2017;47(11):2245-2267.
paper.abstract: A meta-analysis assessed whether wearing compression garments after exercise improved subsequent performance and perceptual or physiological recovery outcomes.
paper.tldr: Compression garments provided small average recovery benefits, with larger effects in some strength and next-day endurance contexts.
paper.methods: Twenty-three studies were synthesized across resistance, running, cycling, and other exercise models, with standardized effects calculated for performance and recovery outcomes.
paper.findings: The overall recovery effect was small. Larger effects appeared for strength recovery more than 24 hours after resistance exercise and for next-day cycling performance, but estimates varied by context.
paper.limitations: Studies were generally small and heterogeneous, and garment pressure, participant training status, and blinding were often unclear.
paper.practicalImplications: Compression garments are a low-burden optional recovery aid, not a substitute for sleep, nutrition, or appropriate load management.
paper.athleteDev: Trial garments with individual athletes and retain them only when comfort, adherence, and the desired next-day outcome justify use.
paper.rtp: The meta-analysis did not validate compression garments as a treatment or clearance criterion for injured athletes.
